q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO?
h: –CHO at the end of the chain is an aldehyde. Count all the carbons, including the CHO carbon.
w: Four carbons with a terminal –CHO: butanal. The CHO carbon counts in the chain, so propanal is wrong; butanone would have the C=O in the middle.
x: Butanone is a ketone, with the C=O inside the chain. A –CHO group sits at the end of the chain.
1-Butanol is an alcohol with –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. This formula has a C=O (–CHO), not an –OH.
Propanal has three carbons. The –CHO carbon counts as part of the chain, so count it too.

q: Methyl ethyl ketone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is a solvent. What is its IUPAC name?
h: Count the carbons (both sides of the C=O). Ketones end in “-one.”
w: Four carbons with a C=O inside the chain: butanone (2-butanone). Butanal is the aldehyde isomer; propanone has only 3 carbons.
x: Butanal is an aldehyde with the C=O at the end of the chain. Here the C=O carbon has a carbon on both sides.
2-Butanol is an alcohol, with –OH instead of C=O. This compound keeps its carbonyl group.
Propanone has only three carbons. Count the carbons on both sides of the C=O.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Number the six-carbon chain from the end that gives the C=O carbon the lower number.
w: Six carbons; numbering from the left puts C=O at C3: 3-hexanone. Numbering from the right gives 4, which is not the lowest number.
x: 4 comes from numbering from the right end. Number from the end that gives the C=O carbon the lower number.
The -al ending is for aldehydes, where the C=O is at the end (always C1). Here the C=O is in the middle of the chain.
3-Pentanone has five carbons. Count every carbon on both sides of the C=O.

q: Acetone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>, mixes completely with water. The best explanation is that
c: water molecules hydrogen bond to acetone's carbonyl oxygen
acetone molecules hydrogen bond to one another
acetone ionizes completely into ions in water
acetone and water are both nonpolar molecules
h: Does acetone have an O–H? If not, can its oxygen still take part in hydrogen bonding with water?
w: Acetone has no O–H, so it cannot H-bond to itself, but its polar C=O oxygen accepts hydrogen bonds from water. That is why small aldehydes and ketones dissolve well yet boil lower than alcohols.
x: Acetone has no O–H (or N–H), so it cannot hydrogen bond to other acetone molecules. Think about what water can supply.
Acetone is a neutral molecule that does not ionize in water. Its solubility comes from attractions between whole molecules.
Water is very polar, and acetone's C=O is polar too. Nonpolar molecules would not mix with water.

q: Which compound is oxidized to propanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, by a mild oxidizing agent?
h: Which carbonyl compound has an H on its C=O carbon that can be replaced by OH?
w: An aldehyde oxidizes easily to the carboxylic acid with the same carbon count: propanal → propanoic acid. Propanone (a ketone) and 2-propanol (which gives a ketone) cannot give a carboxylic acid.
x: Propanone is a ketone: its C=O carbon has no H to replace, so mild oxidation does not affect it.
2-Propanol is a 2° alcohol; oxidation gives a ketone, not a carboxylic acid.
Propane is an alkane with no oxygen. A mild oxidizing agent does not convert it to an acid.

q: Which compound gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent?
h: Tollens' test detects compounds that are easily oxidized: which family?
w: Tollens' reagent (Ag+) oxidizes aldehydes and is reduced to Ag metal (the mirror). Only propanal, CH3CH2CHO, is an aldehyde; ketones such as acetone give no reaction.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> is a ketone (acetone). Ketones are not oxidized by Tollens' reagent, so no silver forms.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> is an alcohol. Tollens' reagent detects a more easily oxidized functional group.
CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> is an ether, which is not oxidized by Tollens' reagent.

q: In a positive Benedict's test for glucose in urine, the blue solution forms a brick-red precipitate of
h: The aldehyde is oxidized, so the copper ion is reduced. Copper(II) becomes copper(I).
w: Cu2+ (blue) is reduced to copper(I) oxide, Cu2O, the brick-red solid. Silver metal is the product of the Tollens' test, not Benedict's.
x: Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> still contains copper(II), which is not reduced. In a positive test the copper ion gains an electron.
CuSO<sub>4</sub> is a blue copper(II) compound that stays dissolved. The red solid forms when copper(II) is reduced.
Silver metal is the mirror from Tollens' test. Benedict's reagent contains copper, not silver.

q: What is formed when butanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is reduced with H<sub>2</sub> and a nickel catalyst?
h: Reduction adds H to each atom of the C=O. Which class of alcohol does a ketone give?
w: Adding H2 across the C=O gives CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, 2-butanol, a 2° alcohol. Reducing a ketone never gives a 1° alcohol, and butanoic acid would be an oxidation product.
x: 1-Butanol has the OH on the end carbon, but in butanone the C=O is on carbon 2. Reduction puts the OH on the former C=O carbon.
Butanal is an aldehyde isomer, not a reduction product. Adding H<sub>2</sub> converts the C=O into C–OH.
Butanoic acid would be an oxidation product, and a ketone cannot form it. H<sub>2</sub> is a reducing agent.

q: A carbon atom bonded to one –OH group and one –OR group (formed when an aldehyde adds one alcohol molecule) is part of a(n)
h: “Hemi” means half: only one alcohol has added.
w: One alcohol adding to the C=O gives a carbon with –OH and –OR: a hemiacetal. An acetal has two –OR groups and no –OH; an ester has a C=O; a hemiketal forms from a ketone, not an aldehyde.
x: An acetal has two –OR groups and no –OH; it forms after a second alcohol adds. Here only one alcohol has added.
An ester has a C=O and an –OR on the same carbon. This carbon has no C=O.
A hemiketal forms from a ketone. The question says the carbonyl compound was an aldehyde.

q: Ethanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CHO, reacts with two molecules of methanol in the presence of acid. What is the organic product?
h: The first methanol gives a hemiacetal; the second replaces the –OH and releases water.
w: With two alcohol molecules and acid, the aldehyde carbon ends up with two –OCH3 groups: CH3CH(OCH3)2, an acetal, plus H2O. The hemiacetal is only the intermediate after one methanol.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)OCH<sub>3</sub> is what forms after only one methanol adds. The question uses two molecules of methanol.
An ester has a C=O, and it forms from a carboxylic acid, not an aldehyde. Here the C=O is used up as alcohols add.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> has only one oxygen and has lost the original carbonyl oxygen. Alcohols add oxygen groups to the carbonyl carbon.

q: Formalin, used to preserve tissue specimens, is an aqueous solution of
h: The “form-” prefix means one carbon. Formalin is an aldehyde solution.
w: Formalin is about 37% methanal, HCHO, in water. Methanol is the alcohol; methanoic acid is formic acid.
x: Methanol is an alcohol, and "formalin" is not named for it. Formalin comes from a one-carbon carbonyl compound.
Methanoic (formic) acid is a carboxylic acid, found in ant stings. Formalin is a solution of a different one-carbon compound.
Acetone (propanone) has three carbons. The "form-" root means one carbon.

q: Which compound is a hemiketal?
h: Find the carbon bonded to two O atoms. Hemi = one –OH and one –OR. Ketal-type carbons have two carbon groups and no H.
w: The carbon in (CH3)2C(OH)OCH3 has one –OH, one –OCH3 and two CH3 groups (it came from acetone + methanol): hemiketal. CH3CH(OH)OCH3 has an H on that carbon (hemiacetal); the two –OCH3 compounds are a ketal and an acetal.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)OCH<sub>3</sub> has an H on the carbon bearing both oxygens, so it came from an aldehyde: that is a hemiacetal.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C(OCH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> has two –OCH<sub>3</sub> and no –OH, so it is a full ketal, not a hemi- compound.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OCH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> has two –OR groups and an H on that carbon: a full acetal from an aldehyde.

q: A carbon atom is bonded to two –OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> groups and two carbon groups (no H, no –OH). This carbon is part of a(n)
h: Two –OR groups means the full product (no hemi). Two carbon groups on that carbon point back to which carbonyl compound?
w: Two –OR groups and no –OH = the second alcohol has added. Two carbon groups (no H) on that carbon means the original carbonyl was a ketone: ketal, formed from a ketone. An acetal's carbon keeps the aldehyde H.
x: An acetal carbon keeps the aldehyde's H. This carbon has two carbon groups and no H.
A hemiketal has one –OH and one –OR. This carbon has two –OR groups and no –OH.
A hemiacetal has an –OH, and its carbon keeps an H. This carbon has neither.

q: Which compound is reduced to 2-pentanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Reduction runs oxidation backward. A secondary alcohol comes from a ketone with C=O on the same carbon.
w: Adding H2 across the C=O of 2-pentanone puts –OH on carbon 2: CH3COCH2CH2CH3. 3-Pentanone gives 3-pentanol, and pentanal or pentanoic acid give the primary alcohol 1-pentanol.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO is an aldehyde; reduction gives a primary alcohol with OH on the end carbon (1-pentanol).
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has its C=O on carbon 3, so reduction gives 3-pentanol. The OH must end up on carbon 2.
A carboxylic acid has its C=O at the end of the chain, so reducing it gives a primary alcohol. The target has OH on carbon 2.

q: Which compound is oxidized to propanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, by a mild oxidizing agent and reduced to 1-propanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, by H<sub>2</sub> and a Ni catalyst?
h: Which compound sits between a 1° alcohol and a carboxylic acid on the oxidation line?
w: An aldehyde sits in the middle of the oxidation line: 1° alcohol ⇌ aldehyde → carboxylic acid. Propanal is oxidized to propanoic acid and reduced to 1-propanol, with the C=O staying on the end carbon.
x: Propanone is a ketone. It is not oxidized by mild oxidizing agents, and its reduction gives 2-propanol, not 1-propanol.
2-Propanol is a 2° alcohol. Oxidizing it gives propanone, a ketone, not propanoic acid.
Propane is an alkane with no oxygen. It is neither oxidized to an acid by a mild oxidizing agent nor reduced by H<sub>2</sub>.

q: The aldehyde (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>CHO contributes to the aroma of cheese and chocolate. Which IUPAC name is correct?
h: The –CHO carbon is always C1 of an aldehyde chain. Count from there to the branch.
w: Start numbering at the –CHO carbon (C1); the chain has 4 carbons and the CH3 branch is on C3: 3-methylbutanal. Numbering from the other end (2-methyl) ignores the rule that the aldehyde carbon is C1.
x: 2-methyl comes from numbering from the branched end. In an aldehyde the –CHO carbon is always C1.
The -one ending is for ketones. A –CHO at the end of the chain is an aldehyde.
The -ol ending is for alcohols. This compound has a –CHO group, not an –OH.

q: A nerve-damaging workplace solvent, methyl butyl ketone, has the structure CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Under IUPAC rules it is called
h: CO in the middle of a condensed formula is a ketone C=O. Number so the carbonyl carbon gets the lowest number.
w: The C=O is on the second carbon of a six-carbon chain, so it is a ketone: 2-hexanone. Counting from the other end (5-hexanone) gives a higher number; hexanal would need a –CHO at the end.
x: Hexanal is an aldehyde with –CHO at the end of the chain. Here the C=O carbon has a CH<sub>3</sub> on one side.
5 comes from numbering from the wrong end. Number so the C=O carbon gets the lowest possible number.
2-Hexanol is an alcohol with –OH. This formula has a C=O, so it is not an alcohol.

q: Catalytic hydrogenation (H<sub>2</sub>, Ni) of pentanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO, gives which compound?
h: Reduction is the reverse of oxidation: H<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=O on the same carbon.
w: H adds to the C and O of the –CHO, so the end carbon becomes –CH2OH: CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2OH (1-pentanol), a 1° alcohol. The carboxylic acid would be an oxidation product.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> has the OH on carbon 2. Reduction puts the OH on the carbon that held the C=O, the end carbon.
The carboxylic acid is an oxidation product. H<sub>2</sub> with Ni is a reduction.
An alkene has no oxygen. H<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=O; it does not remove the oxygen.

q: When 3-methyl-2-butanone, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCOCH<sub>3</sub>, takes up H<sub>2</sub> over platinum, which product and alcohol class result?
h: A ketone's C=O carbon already has two carbon neighbors. What kind of alcohol does it become when C=O becomes CH–OH?
w: The C=O becomes CH–OH on the same carbon: (CH3)2CHCH(OH)CH3. That carbon has two carbons attached, so the product is 3-methyl-2-butanol, a 2° alcohol. Ketones always reduce to 2° alcohols; the skeleton and OH position do not move.
x: The name is right, but check the class. The C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons and one H.
A carboxylic acid would be an oxidation product, and a ketone cannot form one. Adding H<sub>2</sub> is reduction.
This moves the OH to a different carbon. Reduction keeps the oxygen on the same carbon that held the C=O.

q: Hemiacetals form when an aldehyde adds one alcohol molecule. Which structure is a hemiacetal?
h: Find a carbon with two oxygens on it. A hemiacetal carbon has one –OH, one –OR and no C=O.
w: In CH3CH(OH)OCH2CH3 one carbon holds –OH, –OCH2CH3 and an H (it came from an aldehyde plus one ethanol), so it is a hemiacetal. Two –OR groups = acetal; CH3COOCH2CH3 has C=O and –OR on one carbon, so it is an ester; the last choice has –OH and –OR on different carbons.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OCH<sub>3</sub>)OCH<sub>3</sub> has two –OR groups and no –OH, so two alcohol molecules have added: a full acetal.
CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has a C=O and an –OR on the same carbon: that is an ester.
Here the –OH and the –OR are on different carbons, so it is an alcohol and an ether. A hemiacetal has both on one carbon.

q: Which reactants form the ketal (an acetal made from a ketone) CH<sub>3</sub>C(OCH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (with H<sup>+</sup> catalyst)?
h: Remove the two –OR groups and put back a C=O on that carbon. Is it at the end of the chain or in the middle?
w: The carbon with the two –OCH3 groups also has two carbon groups (CH3 and CH2CH3), so it came from a ketone, butanone, CH3COCH2CH3. Each –OCH3 came from methanol: butanone and two CH3OH.
x: Butanal has its C=O at the end of the chain, so it would give an acetal with an H on that carbon. The –OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon here has two carbon groups.
Ethanol would put –OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the carbon. This ketal has –OCH<sub>3</sub> groups.
Alcohols and ethers do not combine to make a ketal. A ketal forms when alcohol molecules add to a C=O.

q: Propanal and butane have the same molar mass but very different boiling points (see table). What best explains the difference?
c: The polar C=O gives propanal dipole–dipole attractions.
Propanal molecules hydrogen bond to one another.
Propanal has much stronger London dispersion forces.
Propanal molecules form ionic bonds to each other.
h: Does propanal have an H on O, N or F? If not, what attraction does a polar bond give?
w: The C=O bond is polar, so propanal has dipole–dipole attractions that butane lacks. Propanal cannot H-bond to itself because it has no O–H; with equal molar masses, the London forces are similar.
x: Propanal has no H on O, N or F, so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself.
London forces depend mostly on molar mass and size. These two have the same molar mass, so their London forces are similar.
Propanal is a neutral covalent molecule; it does not form ions or ionic bonds.

q: In uncontrolled diabetes, a patient's breath can smell like acetone, one of the ketone bodies. Which compound is a ketone?
h: Start at the C=O carbon: a ketone has a carbon on BOTH sides of it.
w: In CH3COCH2CH3 the C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons, so it is a ketone (butanone). –CHO is an aldehyde, –COO– is an ester and C–O–C is an ether.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO ends in –CHO, so its C=O carbon has an H: that is an aldehyde.
CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has a C=O and an –O– on the same carbon: that is an ester.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has no C=O at all; C–O–C is an ether.

q: Butanal reacts with ethanol under acid catalysis, as shown below. This reaction is an example of
h: Look at the product carbon: how many –OR groups and how many –OH groups does it have?
w: One alcohol added across the C=O of an aldehyde, giving a carbon with one –OH and one –OCH2CH3: hemiacetal formation. Acetal formation needs a second alcohol and gives two –OR groups with no –OH.
x: Acetal formation needs a second alcohol and gives two –OR groups with no –OH. Check how many –OH groups the product carbon has.
Esterification uses a carboxylic acid and gives a product with a C=O. Butanal is an aldehyde, and its C=O is used up.
Hydration adds water, giving two –OH groups. Here the reactant adding is ethanol, which brings an –OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Benzaldehyde (almond flavor), shown, is reduced with H<sub>2</sub> and a catalyst under conditions that do not affect the benzene ring. What is the product?
h: Reduction adds H<sub>2</sub> across the C=O. What kind of alcohol does an aldehyde give?
w: H2 adds across C=O, turning the aldehyde CHO into CH2OH: benzyl alcohol, a 1° alcohol. Benzoic acid is the oxidation product (the opposite reaction). Toluene would require removing the oxygen entirely, and the benzene ring is unchanged under these conditions.
x: This drawing is benzoic acid, the oxidation product. H<sub>2</sub> is a reducing agent.
This drawing is toluene: the oxygen is gone completely. H<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=O; it does not remove the oxygen.
This drawing has a cyclohexane ring instead of benzene. The question says the ring is not affected.

q: 3-Pentanone, shown, is reduced with H<sub>2</sub> and a nickel catalyst. What is the product?
h: Reduction converts C=O into CH–OH on the same carbon.
w: H adds to the carbonyl C and O, so C3 becomes CH–OH: 3-pentanol, a 2° alcohol (ketones reduce to 2° alcohols). 2-Pentanol puts the OH on the wrong carbon; pentane removes the oxygen; pentanoic acid is an oxidation product.
x: This drawing is 2-pentanol, with OH on carbon 2. Reduction puts the OH on the carbon that held the C=O, carbon 3.
This drawing is pentane: the oxygen is gone. H<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=O; it does not remove the oxygen.
This drawing is pentanoic acid, an oxidation product. H<sub>2</sub> is a reducing agent, and a ketone cannot give an acid.

q: Propanal reacts with one molecule of methanol in the presence of acid, as shown. What is the product?
h: An aldehyde plus one alcohol gives a hemiacetal: the carbonyl carbon ends up with both –OH and –OR.
w: The CH3O– group of methanol bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O becomes C–OH: a hemiacetal (one OH and one OCH3 on the same carbon). Two OCH3 groups (acetal) need a second methanol. Methyl propanoate is an ester, which forms from a carboxylic acid, not an aldehyde.
x: This drawing has two –OCH<sub>3</sub> groups, which needs two methanol molecules. Only one methanol reacts here.
This drawing is methyl propanoate, an ester with a C=O. Esters form from carboxylic acids; the aldehyde's C=O is used up here.
This drawing is an ether with only one oxygen; the original carbonyl oxygen has disappeared. Adding an alcohol keeps that oxygen.

q: Acetaldehyde (ethanal), shown, reacts with two molecules of ethanol in acid, with loss of water. What is the final product?
h: The first ethanol makes a hemiacetal; the second replaces the –OH with another –OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
w: Ethanal + 2 ethanol → acetal (two –OCH2CH3 groups on the former carbonyl carbon) + H2O. The structure with one OH and one OEt is only the hemiacetal intermediate. Ethyl acetate is an ester, and placing the two OEt groups on different carbons is wrong: both bond to the former carbonyl carbon.
x: This drawing has one –OH and one ethoxy group: the intermediate after one ethanol. The second ethanol replaces the –OH.
This drawing is ethyl acetate, an ester with a C=O. Esters come from carboxylic acids, not aldehydes.
This drawing puts the two ethoxy groups on different carbons. Both alcohols add to the same former carbonyl carbon.

q: Acetone reacts with one molecule of ethanol under acid catalysis. What is the product?
h: A ketone + one alcohol → hemiketal. The former carbonyl carbon ends up with an –OH and an –OR.
w: The ethoxy group adds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O becomes C–OH: a hemiketal (C bonded to OH, OCH2CH3 and two CH3). Two ethoxy groups (ketal) need a second ethanol; the ether has lost an oxygen; the last choice puts the groups on two different carbons.
x: This drawing has two ethoxy groups, which needs two ethanol molecules. Only one ethanol reacts here.
This drawing is an ether with only one oxygen: the carbonyl oxygen has been lost. Adding an alcohol keeps that oxygen as –OH.
This drawing puts the –OH and the ethoxy group on different carbons. Both end up on the former carbonyl carbon.

q: 2-Heptanone is found in blue cheese. What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: Reduction is the reverse of oxidation: H<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=O, which becomes C–OH on the same carbon.
w: H2 adds to the C=O at C2, so a ketone gives a 2° alcohol: 2-heptanol. 1-Heptanol puts the OH on the end carbon, which never held the oxygen. Heptane has lost the oxygen completely, and heptanoic acid is an oxidation product (and would need the C=O at the end).
x: This drawing has the OH on the end carbon, which never held the oxygen. Reduction puts the OH on the former C=O carbon.
This drawing is heptane: the oxygen is gone. H<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=O; it does not remove the oxygen.
This drawing is heptanoic acid, an oxidation product. H<sub>2</sub> is a reducing agent.

q: What is the product of the reaction of 2-methylpropanal shown?
h: An aldehyde is reduced at the CHO carbon. What class of alcohol does that give?
w: H2 adds across the C=O, so –CHO becomes –CH2OH: 2-methyl-1-propanol (isobutyl alcohol), a 1° alcohol. tert-Butyl alcohol puts the OH on the branch carbon, which was never the carbonyl carbon. 2-Methylpropanoic acid is the oxidation product, and 2-methylpropane has lost the oxygen.
x: This drawing puts the OH on the branch carbon, which was never the carbonyl carbon. Reduction keeps the oxygen where the C=O was.
This drawing is 2-methylpropanoic acid, the oxidation product. H<sub>2</sub> is a reducing agent.
This drawing is 2-methylpropane: the oxygen is gone. H<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=O; it does not remove oxygen.

q: Which compound gives 1-phenylethanol, shown, when it is treated with H<sub>2</sub> and a Ni catalyst (the benzene ring does not react)?
h: The OH carbon in the product was the C=O carbon before reduction. Which carbon carries the OH?
w: The OH is on the carbon bonded to the ring, a 2° alcohol carbon, so it came from the ketone acetophenone (C=O on that same carbon). Phenylacetaldehyde gives 2-phenylethanol (OH on the end carbon). 4-Methylbenzaldehyde has the same formula as acetophenone but gives a 1° alcohol. Styrene has no oxygen, so H2 just gives ethylbenzene.
x: This drawing is phenylacetaldehyde, with the C=O on the end carbon. Reducing it gives a 1° alcohol with OH on the end carbon.
This drawing is 4-methylbenzaldehyde: its CHO reduces to a 1° alcohol, CH<sub>2</sub>OH. The product has a 2° alcohol carbon.
This drawing is styrene, which has no oxygen. H<sub>2</sub> would add across its C=C and could not create an –OH.

q: The product of the reaction of 3-methylbutanal shown is partly responsible for foot odor. What is it?
h: Aldehydes oxidize easily: the –CHO carbon gains an O and becomes –COOH. Keep every carbon and branch.
w: The H on the CHO carbon is replaced by OH, giving 3-methylbutanoic acid. 3-Methyl-1-butanol is the reduction product (H2), the opposite reaction. The ketone, 3-methyl-2-butanone, moves the C=O to a different carbon, and 2-methylpropanoic acid has lost a carbon.
x: This drawing is 3-methyl-1-butanol, the reduction product. [O] means oxidation.
This drawing is a ketone with the C=O moved to a different carbon. Oxidation keeps the oxygen on the original –CHO carbon.
This drawing has only four carbons; one carbon is missing. Oxidation keeps every carbon and branch.

q: 2-Hexanone is mixed with a mild oxidizing agent that readily oxidizes aldehydes, as shown. What happens?
h: An aldehyde is oxidized by losing the H on its C=O carbon. Does a ketone have that H?
w: In a ketone the C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons and has no H to lose, so a mild oxidizing agent gives no reaction (this is how Tollens' and Benedict's tests tell aldehydes from ketones). Hexanoic acid is what the aldehyde hexanal would give. 2-Hexanol is a reduction product, and hexanal is an isomer, not a product.
x: This drawing is hexanoic acid, which would come from the aldehyde hexanal. Does 2-hexanone's C=O carbon have an H to lose?
This drawing is 2-hexanol, a reduction product. A mild oxidizing agent cannot add H to the C=O.
This drawing is hexanal, an isomer. An oxidizing agent cannot move the C=O to the end of the chain.

q: Pentanal reacts with one molecule of methanol, as shown. What is the product?
h: One alcohol adds across the C=O: the carbonyl carbon ends up with both an –OH and an –OR.
w: The O of methanol bonds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O becomes C–OH: a hemiacetal, 1-methoxy-1-pentanol. Two –OCH3 groups (an acetal) need a second methanol. Methyl pentanoate is an ester, which forms from a carboxylic acid, and the ether has lost the OH.
x: This drawing has two –OCH<sub>3</sub> groups, which needs two methanol molecules. Only one methanol reacts here.
This drawing is methyl pentanoate, an ester with a C=O. Esters form from carboxylic acids, not aldehydes.
This drawing is an ether with only one oxygen: the carbonyl oxygen has been lost. Adding an alcohol keeps that oxygen as –OH.

q: Butanal reacts with two molecules of methanol, and water is released. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: The first methanol gives a hemiacetal; the second replaces its –OH with another –OCH<sub>3</sub>.
w: The carbonyl O leaves in H2O and the former C=O carbon ends up with two –OCH3 groups: the acetal 1,1-dimethoxybutane. The structure with one OH and one OCH3 is the hemiacetal that forms first. Methyl butanoate is an ester, and the last choice puts the two –OCH3 groups on different carbons.
x: This drawing has an –OH and one –OCH<sub>3</sub>: the intermediate after one methanol. The second methanol replaces the –OH.
This drawing is methyl butanoate, an ester with a C=O. Esters form from carboxylic acids, not aldehydes.
This drawing puts the two –OCH<sub>3</sub> groups on different carbons. Both alcohols add to the same former carbonyl carbon.

q: Cyclohexanone reacts with one molecule of methanol, as shown. What is the product?
h: A ketone plus one alcohol gives a hemiketal: an –OH and an –OR on the former C=O carbon.
w: The methoxy group adds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O becomes C–OH: a hemiketal, 1-methoxycyclohexanol. Two –OCH3 groups (a ketal) need a second methanol. The ether has lost the OH, and 2-methoxycyclohexanol splits the two groups between neighboring carbons.
x: This drawing has two –OCH<sub>3</sub> groups, which needs two methanol molecules. Only one methanol reacts here.
This drawing is an ether with no –OH: the carbonyl oxygen has been lost. Adding an alcohol keeps that oxygen as –OH.
This drawing puts the –OH and the –OCH<sub>3</sub> on neighboring carbons. Both groups end up on the former carbonyl carbon.

q: Cyclopentanone reacts with two molecules of ethanol, and water is released. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: In a ketal, both –OR groups are on the carbon that was the C=O carbon.
w: Two ethanol molecules bond to the carbonyl carbon and the carbonyl O leaves as H2O: the ketal 1,1-diethoxycyclopentane. The structure with an OH and one ethoxy group is only the hemiketal. Putting the ethoxy groups on two different carbons, or keeping only one with no OH, does not match ketal formation.
x: This drawing has an –OH and one ethoxy group: the intermediate after one ethanol. The second ethanol replaces the –OH.
This drawing puts the two ethoxy groups on neighboring ring carbons. Both alcohols add to the same former carbonyl carbon.
This drawing has only one ethoxy group and no –OH; an oxygen has been lost. Two ethanol molecules should add.

q: 5-Hydroxypentanal, shown, has an –OH and a –CHO in the same molecule. In solution it forms a six-membered ring, the same way glucose does. Which structure is the ring form?
h: The –OH oxygen adds to the C=O carbon, forming a cyclic hemiacetal. That carbon keeps an –OH.
w: The O of the –OH bonds to the aldehyde carbon and the C=O becomes C–OH, closing a ring of five C and one O: a cyclic hemiacetal with the OH on the carbon next to the ring O. The C=O version is a cyclic ester (an oxidation product), the ring without an OH has lost an oxygen, and putting the OH on a carbon away from the ring O does not match hemiacetal formation.
x: This drawing keeps a C=O in the ring: a cyclic ester, which is an oxidation product. When the –OH adds, the C=O becomes C–OH.
This ring has no –OH at all, so the carbonyl oxygen has been lost. Adding the –OH to the C=O keeps that oxygen.
This drawing puts the –OH on a carbon that is not next to the ring oxygen. The former C=O carbon bonds to the ring O and keeps the –OH.

q: The five-membered cyclic hemiacetal shown resembles the ring of ribose. Which compound forms it in solution?
h: A cyclic hemiacetal forms when an –OH in the same molecule adds to an aldehyde C=O. Count the ring atoms.
w: The ring has four C and one O. In 4-hydroxybutanal the –OH on C4 can reach the C1 aldehyde carbon, forming exactly that five-membered ring with an OH on the former C=O carbon. 5-Hydroxypentanal gives a six-membered ring. 3-Hydroxybutanal would give a strained four-membered ring with a methyl group. Butanoic acid has no aldehyde.
x: 5-Hydroxypentanal would close a six-membered ring (five C and one O). The ring shown has five atoms.
Here the –OH is on C3, so ring closure gives a four-membered ring with a CH<sub>3</sub> branch. The ring shown has five atoms and no branch.
Butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid with no aldehyde and no separate –OH group. A cyclic hemiacetal needs both in one molecule.

q: 3-Phenylpropanal is reduced under conditions that do not affect the benzene ring. What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: H<sub>2</sub> adds one H to the C and one H to the O of the C=O.
w: The aldehyde –CHO becomes –CH2OH, a 1° alcohol: 3-phenyl-1-propanol. 3-Phenylpropanoic acid is the oxidation product, the opposite reaction. 1-Phenyl-2-propanol has the OH on the wrong carbon, and propylbenzene has lost the oxygen.
x: This drawing is 3-phenylpropanoic acid, the oxidation product. H<sub>2</sub> is a reducing agent.
This drawing puts the OH on the middle carbon of the chain. Reduction keeps the oxygen on the carbon that held the C=O, the end carbon.
This drawing is propylbenzene: the oxygen is gone. H<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=O; it does not remove oxygen.

q: Which carbonyl compound and alcohol react (H<sup>+</sup>) to form the hemiacetal shown?
h: Find the carbon holding both –OH and –OR. It was the C=O carbon; the –OR came from the alcohol.
w: The carbon bonded to both –OH and –OCH2CH3 also carries H and an isopropyl group, so it was the CHO carbon of 2-methylpropanal, and the –OCH2CH3 came from ethanol. The other pairs give isomers (same formula, C6H14O2) in which different groups sit on the oxygen and on the hemiacetal carbon; acetone + 1-propanol gives a hemiketal.
x: Propanal + 2-propanol would put an ethyl on the hemiacetal carbon and an isopropyl on the oxygen. The drawing has these the other way around.
Ethanal + 2-methyl-1-propanol would put a CH<sub>3</sub> on the hemiacetal carbon and a four-carbon group on the oxygen. Check what is on each side.
Acetone is a ketone, so it gives a hemiketal with two carbon groups and no H on that carbon. The drawn carbon has an H.

q: Butanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO, and butanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, are each reduced with H<sub>2</sub> and a Ni catalyst. Which pair of products forms?
c: butanal → butanoic acid; butanone → no reaction
h: Reduction turns the C=O into CH–OH on the same carbon. Where is the C=O in each compound?
w: Reduction adds H2 across the C=O, so the –OH ends up on the carbon that held the C=O. The aldehyde carbon is at the end of the chain, giving a 1° alcohol; the ketone carbon is in the chain, giving a 2° alcohol: 1-butanol and 2-butanol.
x: This swaps the two. The aldehyde's C=O is on the end carbon, so it gives the 1° alcohol.
Butanone's C=O is on carbon 2, so its –OH ends up on carbon 2 as well, giving 2-butanol.
That describes oxidation with a mild oxidizing agent. H<sub>2</sub> with a Ni catalyst reduces both aldehydes and ketones.

q: Which alcohol is formed by reducing an aldehyde?
h: Reduction of a C=O puts an H on the carbonyl carbon. An aldehyde's C=O carbon already has one H, so the product carbon has two H.
w: An aldehyde carbon has one H and one R group; adding H to it gives R–CH2–OH, a primary alcohol such as 1-pentanol. 2-Pentanol and cyclopentanol are secondary alcohols and come from ketones. 2-Methyl-2-butanol is a tertiary alcohol, which cannot be made by reducing any carbonyl compound.
x: This drawing is 2-pentanol: its C–OH carbon has two carbon groups, a 2° alcohol. That comes from reducing a ketone.
This drawing is a 3° alcohol: its C–OH carbon has three carbons and no H. No carbonyl compound reduces to that.
This drawing is cyclopentanol: its C–OH carbon has two ring carbons, a 2° alcohol. That comes from reducing a ketone.

q: The compound shown is a cyclic protecting group used in drug synthesis. Carbon a is bonded to two oxygen atoms. Which term describes it?
c: an acetal carbon: two –OR groups and one H, from an aldehyde
a ketal carbon: two –OR groups and two carbons, from a ketone
a hemiacetal carbon: one –OH and one –OR, from an aldehyde
a hemiketal carbon: one –OH and one –OR, from a ketone
h: Find the carbon bonded to two O atoms. Does either O carry an H? How many carbons are attached to that carbon?
w: Carbon a carries two ring –O–C groups (both are –OR; neither is an –OH), so it is a full acetal/ketal, not a hemi-. It is bonded to only one other carbon (the CH3) plus an H, so it came from an aldehyde (ethanal): an acetal. A ketal carbon would have two carbon groups and no H.
x: A ketal carbon has two carbon groups and no H. Carbon a is bonded to only one carbon (the CH<sub>3</sub>) and carries an H.
A hemiacetal has an –OH. Both oxygens on carbon a are ring –O–C groups; neither has an H.
A hemiketal needs an –OH and two carbon groups on that carbon. Carbon a has neither.

q: In the five-membered ring below, carbon a holds both an OH and a ring oxygen. What kind of carbon is it?
c: a hemiketal carbon: one –OH and one –OR, from a ketone
a hemiacetal carbon: one –OH and one –OR, from an aldehyde
a ketal carbon: two –OR groups, from a ketone
an acetal carbon: two –OR groups, from an aldehyde
h: One of the two oxygens is an OH, so it is a "hemi". Count the carbons on carbon a to decide aldehyde or ketone origin.
w: Carbon a has one –OH and one ring –O–C (an –OR), so it is a hemi- compound; the OH has not yet been replaced. It is bonded to two carbons (the CH3 and the ring CH2) and has no H, so its parent was a ketone: a hemiketal. A hemiacetal carbon would carry an H; acetals and ketals have two –OR groups and no –OH.
x: A hemiacetal carbon keeps the aldehyde's H. Carbon a has no H; count the carbons bonded to it.
A ketal carbon has two –OR groups and no –OH. Carbon a still has an –OH.
An acetal has two –OR groups and no –OH. Carbon a still has an –OH.

q: Which combination of reactants produces a ketal?
c: a ketone and two molecules of alcohol, with loss of water
an aldehyde and two molecules of alcohol, with loss of water
a ketone and one molecule of alcohol
a carboxylic acid and one molecule of alcohol, with loss of water
h: Ketal comes from "ketone"; the "hemi" versions stop after one alcohol.
w: A ketone plus two alcohols (acid catalyst, water removed) gives a ketal: the carbonyl carbon ends up with two –OR groups and two carbon groups. An aldehyde with two alcohols gives an acetal; a ketone with only one alcohol stops at the hemiketal; an acid plus an alcohol gives an ester.
x: An aldehyde plus two alcohols gives an acetal, whose carbon keeps the aldehyde H. The "ket-" in the name points to a different parent.
With only one alcohol, the reaction stops at the hemi- stage, which still has an –OH.
A carboxylic acid plus an alcohol gives an ester, which keeps its C=O.

q: Wildfire smoke that drifts into the Valley contains formaldehyde (methanal, HCHO). Formaldehyde is a gas at room temperature. What best explains its very low boiling point?
c: It is a very small molecule, and it cannot hydrogen bond to other formaldehyde molecules because it has no O–H
It is completely nonpolar, with no dipole
Its molecules hydrogen bond strongly to each other
h: Look for an H bonded to O in HCHO. How big is the molecule?
w: Formaldehyde has a polar C=O, so it has dipole–dipole attractions, but its H atoms are on carbon, so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself, and with only four atoms its dispersion forces are weak. Its attractions are weak, so it boils far below room temperature (about −19 °C).
x: Formaldehyde is a covalent molecule, not an ionic compound. Ionic compounds are solids with very high melting points.
The C=O bond is polar, so formaldehyde does have a dipole. Its low boiling point comes from its small size and the lack of hydrogen bonding.
A hydrogen bond needs an H on O, N or F. Formaldehyde's H atoms are on carbon.
